paragraphs: The administration of government, in its broadest sense, includes all the operations of the body politic, whether legislative, executive, or judiciary. In its most common sense, and perhaps its most precise, however, it is limited to executive details and belongs particularly to the executive department. The actual conduct of foreign negotiations, the preparatory plans of finance, the use and spending of public money in keeping with the general appropriations of the legislature, the organization of the army and navy, and the direction of the operations of war: these and other matters of a similar nature make up what seems most properly to be understood by the administration of government. The persons, therefore, to whose immediate management these different matters are entrusted ought to be regarded as the assistants or deputies of the chief executive. For that reason they ought to receive their offices from his appointment, or at least from his nomination, and ought to be subject to his supervision. This view of the subject at once shows us how closely the length of time the chief executive remains in office is connected with the stability of the system of administration. A successor very often regards reversing and undoing what his predecessor has done as the best proof he can give of his own ability and worth. In addition to this inclination, where the change has come about by public choice, the person put in the place of another is justified in supposing that the dismissal of his predecessor came from a dislike of that man's measures, and that the less he resembles him, the more he will recommend himself to the favor of his constituents. These considerations, together with the influence of personal trust and attachment, would be likely to lead every new President to promote a change of men to fill the subordinate positions. And these causes together could not fail to produce a disgraceful and ruinous instability in the administration of the government.

With a fixed term of considerable length, I connect the circumstance of re-eligibility. The first is necessary to give the officer himself the inclination and the resolution to play his part well, and to give the community time and leisure to observe the tendency of his measures and so to form an estimate of their merits based on experience. The second is necessary to enable the people, when they see reason to approve of his conduct, to continue him in his post, in order to prolong the usefulness of his talents and virtues, and to secure to the government the advantage of permanence in a wise system of administration.

Nothing appears more plausible at first sight, or more ill-founded on close inspection, than a scheme that has had some respectable advocates on the present point. I mean the scheme of keeping the chief executive in office for a certain time and then excluding him from it, either for a limited period or forever after. This exclusion, whether temporary or permanent, would have nearly the same effects, and those effects would for the most part be harmful rather than beneficial.

One bad effect of the exclusion would be a reduction of the inducements to good behavior. There are few men who would not feel much less zeal in the discharge of a duty when they knew that the advantages of the position connected with it must be given up at a fixed time, than when they were allowed to hope to earn a continuance of those advantages by deserving it. This point will not be disputed, so long as it is admitted that the desire of reward is one of the strongest incentives of human conduct, or that the best security for the fidelity of mankind is to make their interests coincide with their duty. Even the love of fame, the ruling passion of the noblest minds, would work against the public good in such a case. If a man could flatter himself with the prospect of being allowed to finish what he had begun, that passion would prompt him to plan and undertake extensive and arduous enterprises for the public benefit, enterprises requiring considerable time to mature and perfect. But when he foresaw that he must leave the scene before he could accomplish the work, and must commit it, together with his own reputation, to hands that might be unequal or unfriendly to the task, that same passion would deter him from the undertaking. The most that can be expected from the generality of men in such a situation is the negative merit of doing no harm, in place of the positive merit of doing good.

Another bad effect of the exclusion would be the temptation to sordid aims, to embezzlement, and, in some instances, to usurpation. An avaricious man who happened to hold the office would look ahead to a time when he must in any event give up the pay he enjoyed. He would feel an inclination, not easy for such a man to resist, to make the best use of his opportunity while it lasted, and he might not hesitate to resort to the most corrupt expedients to make the harvest as abundant as it was brief. The same man, with a different prospect before him, might probably content himself with the regular perquisites of his position, and might even be unwilling to risk the consequences of abusing his opportunities. His avarice might be a guard upon his avarice. Add to this that the same man might be vain or ambitious, as well as avaricious. If he could expect to prolong his honors by his good conduct, he might hesitate to sacrifice his appetite for them to his appetite for gain. But with the prospect before him of approaching and inevitable extinction, his avarice would be likely to defeat his caution, his vanity, or his ambition.

An ambitious man, too, would find himself seated on the summit of his country's honors. He would look ahead to the time when he must descend forever from that exalted height, and would reflect that no exertion of merit on his part could save him from the unwelcome reversal. Such a man, in such a situation, would be much more strongly tempted to seize a favorable opportunity to attempt to prolong his power, at every personal risk, than if he had a reasonable prospect of reaching the same end by doing his duty.

Would it promote the peace of the community, or the stability of the government, to have half a dozen men who had enjoyed enough credit to be raised to the seat of the highest executive office wandering among the people like discontented ghosts, sighing for a place they were destined never to possess again?

A third bad effect of the exclusion would be to deprive the community of the benefit of the experience the chief executive has gained in the exercise of his office. That experience is the parent of wisdom is a saying whose truth the wisest and the simplest of mankind alike recognize. What is more desirable or more essential than this quality in the governors of nations? Where is it more desirable or more essential than in the chief executive of a nation? Can it be wise to put this desirable and essential quality under the ban of the Constitution, and to declare that the moment it is acquired, its possessor shall be forced to abandon the position in which he acquired it and to which it is suited? Yet this is the precise meaning of all those regulations that exclude men from serving their country, by the choice of their fellow citizens, after they have fitted themselves, through a course of service, to do so with greater usefulness.

A fourth bad effect of the exclusion would be the banishing of men from positions in which, in certain emergencies of the state, their presence might be of the greatest importance to the public interest or safety. There is no nation that has not, at one time or another, found an absolute necessity for the services of particular men in particular situations. Perhaps it would not be too strong to say that this necessity has extended to the preservation of its political existence. How unwise, therefore, must be every such self-denying ordinance as forbids a nation to use its own citizens in the manner best suited to its needs and circumstances! Even without supposing that any one man is personally indispensable, it is evident that a change of chief executive, at the outbreak of a war or in any similar crisis, would at all times harm the community, even if the replacement were a man of equal merit. It would put inexperience in the place of experience, and would tend to unsettle and throw into confusion the already established course of the administration.

A fifth bad effect of the exclusion would be that it would operate as a constitutional prohibition of stability in the administration. By making a change of men in the first office of the nation necessary, it would make a change of measures necessary. It is not generally to be expected that men will change and measures remain the same. The contrary is the usual course of things. And we need not fear that there will be too much stability while the option of changing still exists. Nor need we wish to forbid the people from continuing their confidence where they think it may safely be placed, and where, by their constancy, they may avoid the fatal problems of shifting councils and a changeable policy.

These are some of the disadvantages that would flow from the principle of exclusion. They apply most forcibly to the scheme of permanent exclusion. But when we consider that even a partial exclusion would always make the person's readmission a remote and uncertain prospect, the observations that have been made will apply almost as fully to one case as to the other.

What advantages are promised to offset these disadvantages? They are represented to be: first, greater independence in the chief executive; second, greater security to the people. Unless the exclusion is permanent, there will be no pretense for inferring the first advantage. But even in that case, may he not have some object beyond his present position, to which he may sacrifice his independence? May he not have connections and friends for whom he may sacrifice it? May he not be less willing to make personal enemies by firm conduct, when he acts under the impression that a time is fast approaching when he not only MAY, but MUST, be exposed to their resentment, on an equal footing with them, or perhaps an inferior one? It is not an easy point to determine whether his independence would be more promoted or more impaired by such an arrangement.

As to the second supposed advantage, there is still greater reason to doubt it. If the exclusion were permanent, a man of irregular ambition, the only kind of man about whom there could be reason in any case to feel apprehension, would yield with infinite reluctance to the necessity of taking leave forever of a post in which his passion for power and pre-eminence had grown into habit. And if he had been fortunate or skillful enough to win the good will of the people, he might induce them to regard as a very odious and unjustifiable restraint upon themselves a provision designed to deprive them of the right to give a fresh proof of their attachment to a favorite. Circumstances can be imagined in which this disgust of the people, backing the thwarted ambition of such a favorite, might produce greater danger to liberty than could ever reasonably be feared from the possibility of a continuation in office, by the voluntary votes of the community exercising a constitutional privilege.

There is an excess of refinement in the idea of depriving the people of the ability to keep in office men who had earned, in the people's own opinion, their approval and confidence. The advantages of this idea are at best speculative and doubtful, and are outweighed by disadvantages far more certain and decisive.
